## Answer: **Final blood vs Baseline blood shows negligible effects.**

It is lowest on every metric, in all 8 variant × p₀ cells, under both decision rules.

## Primary table (30v30, p0 from top-100-trimmed matrix)

| comparison | testable genes | raw p<0.05 | BH p<0.05 | BH prop | BH & \|log2FC\|>1 | med \|log2FC\| | p90 \|log2FC\| |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **final blood vs baseline blood** | 22,060 | 16,336 | **16,061** | 0.728 | **1,224** | **0.264** | **0.809** |
| dentate gyrus vs baseline blood | 23,017 | 20,113 | 20,026 | 0.870 | 13,408 | 1.309 | 5.831 |
| dentate gyrus vs final blood | 22,890 | 19,998 | 19,941 | 0.871 | 13,512 | 1.344 | 5.914 |

## Your three pinned-down items

1. **Responder pooling.** Primary is pooled 30v30; the **Control-only 10v10 run does NOT flip the ranking — it widens the gap** (12,767 vs 18,618/18,686 BH-significant). Nothing to surface as contradictory.
2. **Outlier library.** Leave-`Control_dentate_gyrus5`-out moves the DG contrasts by <0.5% (20,026→19,985; 19,941→19,916) and cannot touch the blood contrast by construction. It neither manufactures nor masks the effect.
3. **Expression filter, stated explicitly:** keep genes with `max(arm A mean, arm B mean) ≥ 1.0` normalised count, in addition to the zero-in-both drop. Testable genes fall to 17,817–19,772; ranking unchanged (15,520 vs 19,072/18,967).

## Ranking stability (the acceptance criterion)

BH counts, all 4 variants × 2 p₀ constructions: **8/8 cells put final-vs-baseline blood lowest**; the **BH rule and raw-p rule never disagree**; minimum 2nd/1st margin across all cells = **1.172×**. Untrimmed p₀ shifts absolute counts (16,061→16,849) but not the ordering. Full grid in `results/summary_binomial_dge.csv`, `results/rank_bh_variants.csv`, `results/rank_raw_variants.csv`.

## Evidence the machinery isn't self-generating the answer

- **Independent p-value verification:** recomputed 4 random genes from the CSV with a separate betainc implementation → exact agreement (e.g. Fyttd1 k=20792, n=40974, p=3.836e-61 both). The test function itself matched R's `binom.test` central convention to 4e-15 over 500 random cases; computed in log space so nothing underflows.
- **Effect sizes tell the same story as counts:** median |log2FC| 0.26 vs 1.31/1.34; >2-fold genes 1,224 vs 13,408/13,512 (~11×).
- **Marker check:** Prox1 5.4/1737.7/3.1, Calb1 4.4/3040.3/4.5, Cd19 4236/0.3/3458 (baseline/DG/final) — DG is the odd tissue out, the two blood timepoints are alike.
- **Permutation null:** random 15v15 splits within one tissue yield 4,482–7,938 BH-significant genes, i.e. the pooled binomial over-calls badly. Against each contrast's own floor (mean of its two arms) final-vs-baseline sits at 2.19×, DG-vs-baseline 3.56×, DG-vs-final 3.21× — same ordering.
- **DESeq blocks used as anchor only**, never as the result.

## Limitations to keep in the write-up

- NormCount is size-factor **normalised and fractional** (68.1% non-integer), so rounding makes this a **model approximation, not an exact test on true discrete counts**.
- The pooled binomial treats 60 libraries as 60 Bernoulli draws — no biological dispersion, pairing by animal discarded — so absolute counts are inflated (permutation null proves it). Only relative ordering is interpretable, which is what the question asks.
- **"Negligible" is relative**: this contrast is still 72.8% "significant" by count. It is negligible against the tissue contrasts, and independently small in absolute effect size (median |log2FC| 0.26; only 5.6% of genes >2-fold).

## Deliverables
`analysis/run_binomial_dge.py` + `analysis/inspect_workbook.py` (both executed), `results/REPORT.md`, `results/summary_binomial_dge.csv`, `results/rank_bh_variants.csv`, `results/rank_raw_variants.csv`, three per-gene CSVs (`results/deg_*.csv`, 16 columns incl. k/n/p0/log2FC/pval/padj_BH/flags), `results/run_log.txt`.

payload.answer: Final blood vs Baseline blood shows negligible effects (lowest significant-gene count and by far the smallest fold-change distribution in all 8 variant x p0 checks); the two dentate gyrus contrasts show massive effects.
